record.paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
record.original_question: Can semi-analytic models with radio-mode AGN feedback achieve quantitative agreement with the observed star-formation histories of massive elliptical galaxies, rather than only reproducing the qualitative trend that more massive ellipticals have shorter star-formation time-scales?

evidence.quote: Therefore these models seem to reproduce, at least qualitatively, the observed trend for more massive ellipticals to have shorter star formation time-scales.
A good quantitative agreement has not been shown yet and is complicated by large uncertainties associated to star formation histories extracted from observed galaxy spectra.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider semi-analytic models of galaxy formation built on hierarchical merger trees of dark-matter halos, in which baryonic processes (gas cooling, star formation, supernova feedback, galaxy mergers, chemical enrichment) are evolved by coupled differential/algebraic recipes, and in which "radio-mode" active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback is included as an energy-injection term that suppresses gas cooling in massive halos hosting a central supermassive black hole accreting in a low-accretion-rate (radio) state.

For each model galaxy, define its star-formation history (SFH) as the function ψ(t) giving the star-formation rate as a function of cosmic time, and its star-formation time-scale τ_SF (e.g., the e-folding time of ψ(t) or the time over which a fixed fraction of the present-day stellar mass was assembled). Let M_⋆ denote the present-day stellar mass of a galaxy classified as a massive elliptical (M_⋆ ≳ 10^{11} M_⊙).

Observationally, the SFHs of massive ellipticals (as inferred from spectral fitting of their stellar populations) exhibit "downsizing": more massive ellipticals form their stars earlier and on shorter time-scales τ_SF. Existing semi-analytic models with radio-mode AGN feedback reproduce this trend qualitatively (i.e., dτ_SF/dM_⋆ < 0).

Problem. Determine whether one can construct a semi-analytic galaxy-formation model with radio-mode AGN feedback whose predicted distribution of star-formation histories ψ(t | M_⋆) for massive elliptical galaxies matches the observationally inferred SFHs not only qualitatively but quantitatively — that is, agrees within observational uncertainties on the mean formation epoch ⟨t_form⟩(M_⋆) and the star-formation time-scale τ_SF(M_⋆) as functions of stellar mass.
artifact.status_search_result: The question concerns whether semi-analytic models with radio-mode AGN feedback can achieve quantitative (not just qualitative) agreement with observed star-formation histories of massive ellipticals. Subsequent literature (e.g., works on downsizing, archaeological SFHs vs. SAM predictions, and AGN-feedback prescriptions in models such as Henriques et al. and Croton et al. updates) has continued to report tensions: SAMs reproduce downsizing trends qualitatively but still struggle to match observed SFH shapes and time-scales quantitatively, with large observational uncertainties persisting. No definitive resolution has been published, so the problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Galaxy formation: Semi-analytic models confront observations (review)
status_evidence.snippet: Semi-analytic models reproduce downsizing qualitatively, but quantitative match to inferred SFHs of massive ellipticals remains challenging due to feedback uncertainties and SFH-extraction systematics.
status_evidence.claim: Quantitative agreement between SAMs with AGN feedback and observed SFHs of massive ellipticals is not yet achieved.

status_evidence.title: Henriques et al., Galaxy formation in the Planck cosmology
status_evidence.snippet: Updated Munich SAM with radio-mode AGN feedback fits stellar mass functions and passive fractions; residual discrepancies in the timing/duration of star formation in massive galaxies remain.
status_evidence.claim: Improved SAMs still show residual mismatches in star-formation timescales of massive ellipticals.
